title: Merchant Payment: Meaning, Processing Flow, Fees and Settlement Explained
summary: What is a merchant payment? Learn how businesses accept customer payments, what a merchant account does, which fees may apply and when funds settle.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


Merchant payment processing is the system that enables a business to accept customer payments, route transaction information for authorization, and receive the funds after settlement. It connects the checkout experience with payment gateways, processors, acquiring institutions, payment networks, and the merchant’s designated bank account.


In everyday usage, “merchant payment” may refer either to a customer payment accepted by a business or to the later settlement of funds to the merchant. This guide explains the payment-processing flow, merchant accounts, outlets, fees, and settlement process in simple terms.


##


**What is Merchant Payment?**


A merchant payment is a payment a customer makes to a business for goods or services, whether through UPI, a card, net banking or another accepted method. The business can see a successful payment before the proceeds reach its bank account. That later transfer is called merchant settlement. A gateway or POS system, banks, payment networks and sometimes a payment aggregator support the flow, depending on the method used.


From the customer’s perspective, it is a purchase payment; from the business’s perspective, it is a merchant payment or collection. Payment success and settlement are different stages: the transaction can succeed at checkout while the provider transfers the eligible funds to the business bank account later. The payment method and provider determine the exact route.


***Also read:[How payment gateways and processors differ](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/difference-between-payment-gateway-and-payment-processor/)***


##


How Does Merchant Payment Work?


The payment flow begins when a customer chooses a payment method at checkout and ends when the transaction amount is settled to the merchant according to the applicable settlement cycle.


1. The customer initiates the payment at the checkout page using a card, bank transfer,[digital wallet](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/types-of-e-payment-systems/) , or[UPI](https://www.cashfree.com/upi-payment-gateway/) .
2. For an online transaction, the gateway securely captures or transmits the necessary payment information to the relevant processor or payment system. The exact route differs for cards, UPI, net banking and wallets.
3. The relevant bank, issuer or payment system checks the transaction and returns a successful, failed or pending status according to the payment method and its rules.
4. An approved transaction is recorded and processed for clearing. The payment network, acquirer, processor, or payment aggregator performs the applicable transaction handling and reconciliation steps.
5. During settlement, the amount due to the merchant is credited to the designated bank account after applicable processing fees, refunds, disputes, taxes, and other adjustments.


[RBI](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/NotificationUser.aspx?Id=11822&Mode=0) distinguishes payment aggregators, which facilitate merchant connections with acquirers and handle the movement of funds, from payment gateways, which provide technology infrastructure without handling funds.


##


**Types of Merchant Payment Processing**


Merchant payment processing can be classified by the payment method, whether the customer is physically present, and the technology or payment rail used. The same business may use several types at once.


**Card-based Merchant Payment Processing:** A common merchant payment processing covering credit cards,[debit cards](https://www.cashfree.com/debit-card-emi/) , and prepaid cards. They are further divided into two types.


1. **Card Present (In-Person) Processing:** These transactions occur at physical locations through terminals, card readers, and[POS services](https://www.cashfree.com/soft-pos/) .


2. **Card Not Present Processing:** Includes payments where the card is not physically present, and payments are made through phone or online mode.


**Bank account-based merchant payments:** Customers may pay through UPI, net banking, NEFT, IMPS or RTGS, depending on the channel the business supports. These methods do not all have the same confirmation or settlement timing. A provider may still be involved in payment acceptance, reporting and reconciliation.


**Mobile Payment Processing:** Mobile payment processing enables businesses to accept payments through mobile devices, QR codes, mobile apps, or softPOS solutions. Availability, authentication, and settlement depend on the payment method and provider.


##


Merchant Payment Processing Fees Explained


The fees a merchant pays depend on the provider, payment method, transaction type, geography, risk profile, and commercial agreement. The following are possible fee components; not every provider or merchant will incur every fee.


Possible fee What it covers


Processing or transaction fee A percentage, fixed amount or combination charged on an eligible payment


Card interchange and network costs Card issuing and network costs, where relevant to the provider’s pricing model


Gateway or platform fee Payment technology and related services, if charged separately


Refund or dispute fee Charges or adjustments that may apply under the contract


POS or equipment fee Terminal purchase, rental or service, if used


Cross-border or conversion cost International acceptance and currency conversion, where applicable


Account or subscription fee Recurring service charges, if part of the plan


Compare the fee schedule for the payment methods your customers actually use. For the bundled percentage a merchant may pay, see[merchant discount rate (MDR)](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/merchant-discount-rate-mdr/) .


##


**Online and Offline Merchant Payment Example**


Payments between merchants and customers happen online, where the customers pay sitting at home, or offline when they pay at the store through POS. In both cases, how the payment is processed, tracked, and settled differs.


###


**Online Merchant Payment – eCommerce**


Let’s say a customer places an online order worth ₹1,000 on an e-commerce website and completes payment using a debit or credit card. The payment gateway and processor handle the transaction, securely transmitting the payment details for authorization. Once approved, the transaction is recorded, but the merchant does not receive the funds immediately.


Once the ₹1,000 payment succeeds, the transaction appears in the merchant’s payment records. The provider later settles the eligible amount to the business bank account. The net credit may be lower than ₹1,000 if the agreement provides for fees, taxes or other adjustments; it need not be lower in every case. Match the payment, deductions and bank credit during[payment reconciliation](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/ecommerce-payment-reconciliation/) .


###


**Offline Merchant Payment – POS or Retail**


When shopping in a physical store, customers pay with their cards or use UPI at the[POS terminal](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/digitizing-pos-payments/) to complete the purchase. This transaction is again linked to the merchant account, and all payments made through the POS portal will end up in the designated account.


A POS system can help merchants track payments by location. Card and UPI payments may follow different processing and settlement routes, and the provider may group eligible transactions into settlement batches. The timing depends on the merchant’s arrangement and any faster settlement options.


The settled amount after fee deductions is credited to the merchant’s account, with reports showing which outlet generated the payment. This outlet-level mapping is critical for reconciliation, accounting, and multi-store operations.


***Also read:[Retail payment processing across POS, QR and online checkout](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/retail-payment-processing/)***


##


**Merchant Account – Meaning, Purpose & Role in Payment Flow**


In traditional card acquiring, a merchant account is an account or arrangement used to identify and process a business’s card payments before the proceeds are transferred to its bank account. In other setups, a payment aggregator can onboard the business without requiring it to open a separate merchant account directly with an acquiring bank.


*No merchant payments can be completed without a merchant account. The merchant account acts as an intermediary layer that holds the money until and unless all steps, including authorization,[risk checks, chargebacks](https://www.cashfree.com/risk-shield-payment-gateway/) , and settlement processing, are complete.*


In practice, the merchant account serves as a control layer for payment risk and fund movement. It allows acquiring banks and processors to manage fraud exposure, apply fees and reversals, and handle chargebacks before funds are released to the merchant’s bank account. This structure protects both the payment network and the merchant while ensuring settlements are processed accurately.


A merchant account is not the same as a business bank account. While the business bank account is where settled funds are ultimately deposited, the merchant account is used to process and manage transactions during the payment lifecycle. The payment gateway connects the checkout experience to the merchant account, transmitting transaction data securely so payments can be authorized and later settled.


##


**Merchant Outlet Meaning in Multi-Store Businesses**


A merchant outlet is a business location, which can be a physical store or an online platform, where merchants sell goods and accept payments. These can be online or offline payments made through cards, bank transfers, or through POS machines.


Multi-store businesses may configure outlets under one provider relationship to separate payment activity by location. Account structure and reporting vary by provider. This setup allows businesses to scale operations without managing multiple merchant accounts, while still maintaining clear visibility into outlet-level performance.


- An outlet may be mapped to a POS terminal, QR code, online channel or other collection point.
- The transactions flow through the same merchant account, leading to authorization and settlement.
- All transactions are then detailed out through comprehensive reporting and reconciliation.


A provider may offer central reporting while identifying the outlet for each transaction. Confirm whether settlement reports are available by outlet, by bank account or only for the overall business before promising location-level reports. These reports make it easier to track revenue, reconcile payments, and manage audits.


##


**Conclusion**


A merchant payment begins when a customer pays a business. The transaction can be marked successful before the eligible funds are settled to the business bank account. Understanding that gap helps merchants compare fees, plan cash flow and reconcile sales with bank credits.


The setup depends on the payment methods and provider. Some businesses use an acquiring arrangement and merchant account; others use a payment aggregator. Multi-outlet businesses should also check how each store or channel appears in reports. For a closer look at timing, see the[payment settlement cycle guide](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-settlement-cycle-explained/) .

##


FAQs on Merchant Payment


####


What is merchant payment?


A merchant payment is a payment a customer makes to a business for goods or services. It may be made by UPI, card, net banking or another accepted method. Settlement is the later transfer of eligible funds to the business’s bank account.


####


What is the difference between merchant payment and customer payment?


They describe the same purchase from different sides: the customer pays and the merchant receives the payment. Settlement is a separate later stage in which the provider transfers eligible funds to the business bank account.


####


How long does merchant payment settlement take?


There is no universal T+1 to T+3 period. Timing depends on the provider, payment method, merchant agreement, bank working days and any faster settlement option. Check the schedule in your account and distinguish payment success from bank credit.


####


What is a merchant account?


In a traditional acquiring setup, a merchant account is a business payment-processing arrangement linked to an acquirer. It is distinct from the bank account that receives settlement. Businesses using an aggregator may not need a separate direct acquiring account.


####


Can a business have multiple merchant outlets under one account?


Often yes, if the provider supports multiple outlet or channel identifiers. Confirm how each outlet’s payments and settlements appear in the reporting tools.
